# Eleven green end-to-end runs while checkout was broken in every one of them

## Problem Description

Larder is our React Native grocery app. Build 412 went out on Tuesday and
support had 40 tickets by Thursday morning: you tap **Place order**, the order
is created, and then the app sits on a blank white screen forever. The
confirmation screen throws on render because the orders API renamed
`order.reference` to `order.referenceCode` back in build 401 and nobody updated
the screen. That part is understood and a fix is already in review — I am not
asking about the app bug, and I do not want anyone touching
`app/OrderConfirmationScreen.jsx`.

What I have to explain to my director on Monday is the CI history. The
end-to-end job on `main` ran eleven times between build 401 and build 412 and
was green all eleven times. `e2e/checkout.test.js` taps through the basket,
places an order, and checks the confirmation screen and the reference printed
on it. The confirmation screen has not rendered since the second of July.

Two people have opinions and I have to answer both of them by Monday:

- Priya wants `testTimeout` in the Jest config raised from two minutes to five.
  Her theory is that the CI simulators are slower than our laptops and things
  are being cut off before they finish.
- Marcus wrote a `settle()` helper — three seconds of waiting after a tap — and
  merged it into `e2e/account.test.js` three weeks ago. That file has needed
  nothing since, which is more than anyone else can say, and he wants it across
  the other 11 spec files before 1.9.0. Nobody has offered an alternative and I
  am fairly close to letting him do it.

Four spec files are attached, along with the run history, the Jest config, the
confirmation screen and the promo banner component. Tell me why the job did not
go red on any of the eleven builds, and give me back specs I can trust.

## Output Specification

1. Go through the four attached spec files and repair any that would not have
   gone red on build 412. Leave alone any that are already sound, and do not
   change which behaviours a spec checks or delete a spec.
2. Write `docs/why-eleven-runs-were-green.md` explaining the CI history, and
   give me your answer on Marcus's helper and on Priya's timeout so I can put it
   in writing on Monday.
3. Say in that document what the remaining 8 spec files need from us.
evals.expected_output:
1. Go through the four attached spec files and repair any that would not have
   gone red on build 412. Leave alone any that are already sound, and do not
   change which behaviours a spec checks or delete a spec.
2. Write `docs/why-eleven-runs-were-green.md` explaining the CI history, and
   give me your answer on Marcus's helper and on Priya's timeout so I can put it
   in writing on Monday.
3. Say in that document what the remaining 8 spec files need from us.
assertions: docs/why-eleven-runs-were-green.md exists, answers Marcus and Priya separately, and says what the remaining 8 spec files need. A document that addresses only one of the two people scores at most half.

The document states that the wait chains in e2e/checkout.test.js are unterminated, so awaiting them resolves immediately on an object that never ran the wait and never checked anything — the spec could not fail whatever the app did. Attributing the eleven green runs to slow simulators, to intermittency, to the app bug being caught elsewhere, or to a missing assertion library scores zero. Saying the waits 'are missing a timeout' without stating that the assertion therefore never ran, so the file was incapable of reporting a failure, scores at most half. Citing the 0.9s duration against the four-second manual timing is not required for full marks but a document that reaches the conclusion with no evidence from the run history scores at most half.

`does not show an error for a valid promo code` asserts against `promo-error`, which no component renders — app/PromoBanner.jsx renders `promo-error-banner` — so the check passes because the element is absent rather than because the app is correct. Full marks require repairing the spec to name the identifier that exists (or otherwise making the check able to fail) AND saying in the document that an absence assertion against a non-existent identifier is always green. Leaving promos.test.js untouched scores zero. Editing it without noticing the identifier mismatch — for example only adding a wait — scores zero.

MUST NOT endorse rolling `settle()` across the other spec files, and MUST NOT leave the existing calls in e2e/account.test.js in place: fixed sleeps between actions mask real synchronisation problems rather than fix them. Approving the rollout, or approving it 'as a temporary measure until the specs are repaired', scores zero. Removing the calls from account.test.js but giving no verdict on the rollout scores at most half.

After the sleeps come out, `uploads an avatar` must still tolerate the 9.4-13.8s CDN upload the report measures — an explicit bounded wait on the avatar image with a timeout comfortably above that range. Deleting the three sleeps and leaving the bare assertion scores zero: the default assertion timeout is far shorter than the measured upload and the spec that was passing now fails. Substituting a different fixed sleep scores zero. Choosing a timeout at or under the measured range scores at most half.

MUST NOT change `testTimeout` in e2e/jest.config.js. Nothing in the job has ever approached the two-minute limit — the whole suite finishes in 44 seconds — so the change addresses a failure mode that is not occurring. Landing the config change scores zero. Declining it without saying why it cannot be the cause scores at most half.

MUST NOT modify e2e/search.test.js, which uses plain auto-waiting assertions and would have gone red on build 412 already, and MUST NOT modify app/OrderConfirmationScreen.jsx, which the request rules out. Any edit to either scores zero here.

# Nineteen specs went red the Monday we shipped German

## Problem Description

We shipped `de-DE` and `ar-EG` alongside `en-US` on Monday. The app is fine.
The end-to-end suite is not: on a simulator set to German, 19 of our 26 specs
fail. On `en-US` they are all green, same build, same binary. Arabic is worse.

Rasmus was contracting with us through August and sent a patch on his last day.
It imports our translation catalogue into the spec files and looks every string
up through it, so a German run asks the catalogue for the German string. I ran
it: German goes from 19 failures to 2, Arabic from 21 to 3. It is the only
thing anyone has produced, it is clever, and it is queued to merge on Friday.
If it should not go in I need something concrete to say, because "this feels
wrong" is not going to beat a patch that turns 19 red specs green.

Two other things you should know before you answer.

Marketing are rewriting the catalogue copy this quarter. "Add to cart" becomes
"Add to basket" in October, in all three locales, and the checkout wording is
being shortened at the same time.

And there are two specs that have been failing on the Android emulator for
about a month, in English, on the same build that is green on the iOS
simulator. We shelved them as "an Android thing" and stopped looking. They are
in the attached run summary. Sort those out too while you are in the file.

The two spec files, the components they touch, the run summary, Rasmus's patch
and the changelog for the date-picker package we use are attached. Our money
formatter and its unit tests are there because one of the failures is about a
price string.

## Output Specification

1. Make `e2e/catalogue.test.js` and `e2e/checkout.test.js` green on all three
   locales and on both platforms. Do not change which behaviour a spec checks.
2. Change files under `app/` if your fix needs it.
3. Write `docs/suite-locale-decision.md`: your verdict on Rasmus's patch with
   the reasoning, the rule you want the team to follow instead, and your
   explanation of the two long-standing Android failures.
evals.expected_output:
1. Make `e2e/catalogue.test.js` and `e2e/checkout.test.js` green on all three
   locales and on both platforms. Do not change which behaviour a spec checks.
2. Change files under `app/` if your fix needs it.
3. Write `docs/suite-locale-decision.md`: your verdict on Rasmus's patch with
   the reasoning, the rule you want the team to follow instead, and your
   explanation of the two long-standing Android failures.
assertions: Both spec files are edited and docs/suite-locale-decision.md exists carrying a verdict on the patch, the replacement rule, and an explanation of the Android pair. A document missing the Android explanation scores at most half.

Full marks require a stable identifier placed on the host View that wraps `<NativeDateTimePicker>` in app/DeliveryDateField.jsx — or on some other element the spec can address that is not the vendor component itself — the spec addressing that identifier instead of the translated accessibility label, and the document stating why the obvious placement fails: the 3.0.0 changelog forwards only an allow-listed set of props to the native view and drops the rest, and `testID` is not on that list. Putting `testID` on `<NativeDateTimePicker>` scores zero for this criterion — it looks correct and leaves the element unreachable. Leaving the spec matching on the translated `Delivery date` label scores zero. Getting the placement right with no explanation of the constraint scores at most half.

MUST NOT merge patches/i18n-lookup.diff or adopt its technique as the team's rule for locating elements. A selector that reads from the same catalogue the screen renders from agrees with the screen by construction: it stays green through a wrong, missing or untranslated string, and it has to be re-edited every time marketing rewrites copy — the October `Add to basket` change is the case in hand. Merging the patch, or endorsing it as an interim measure, scores zero. Rejecting it on taste with no statement of what it stops the suite from catching scores at most half.

Both long-standing failures match on the view class `RCTImageView`, which is why they are green on the iOS simulator and red on the Android emulator on the same build. Full marks require replacing both matchers with stable identifiers placed on the two images in app/ProductCard.jsx and app/DeliveryDateField.jsx, and naming the cause in the document. Leaving either class-name matcher in place scores zero. Repairing the locale failures and leaving the Android pair unexplained scores zero. Making the matcher platform-conditional rather than giving the images identifiers scores at most half.

The subtotal on screen is a locale-formatted number produced by src/format-money.js, not catalogue copy. Full marks require the spec to address the amount through a stable identifier and to compare it against what that same formatter returns for the run's locale. Still asserting the literal `'$4.99'`, or any other hardcoded currency string, scores zero. Dropping the value and asserting only that the row is visible scores at most half. A document that rules out importing any app module into a spec scores at most half here — a unit-tested number format is not user-visible copy, and this is the one place the patch's technique is sound.

The document must state that accessibility labels in this app are translated exactly as visible text is — `t('nav.cart')`, `t('checkout.deliveryDate')`, `t('badge.organic')` — so moving a selector from visible text to the label buys nothing. Replacing a text selector with a label selector on the same translated string anywhere in the two spec files scores zero for this criterion.
MUST NOT modify src/format-money.js or test/format-money.test.js; the formatter is correct and its behaviour is what the German failure output describes. Any edit to either scores zero here.

evals.prompt:
# A fresh install before every spec fixed the order-dependence and tripled our CI bill

## Problem Description

Our React Native app has ten end-to-end spec files. Run any one of them on its
own and it is green. Run the whole suite and everything from the third file
onwards falls over with `element(by.id('home-search')) not found` — because the
file before it finished on the order-detail screen and the next one starts by
assuming it is on home. Classic, and entirely our fault.

Two weeks ago a contractor fixed it. His change puts a full uninstall and
reinstall of the app in the shared `beforeEach`, so every spec starts from a
virgin install. It does work — the suite has been green every night since.

It also took the suite from **4m12s to 44m56s**, and our macOS runner minutes
for September are already 2.9x August. Finance noticed before we did. The
contractor's contract ended last Friday.

I want this reverted, but I do not want the order-dependence back, and there is
a complication. Before he arrived, Dana tried the obvious cheap alternative —
resetting the app between specs without reinstalling — and some files broke that
had been fine. She could not work out why, gave up after an afternoon, and that
is part of why we ended up with the reinstall for everything. Her results from
that attempt are in the timings report.

So: get me back to something that runs in single-digit minutes and keeps the
suite order-independent. What I would really like is one rule that applies to
every spec file, because bespoke setup per file is exactly how we got into this
— ten different answers to "how does a spec start" is the state I am trying to
leave, and every exception is a thing the next person has to learn.

The shared hooks, five of the ten spec files and the timings report are
attached, along with the onboarding module and its unit tests.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `e2e/init.js` so the suite no longer reinstalls the app before every
   spec.
2. Edit any spec files that need to change as a consequence of that.
3. Write `docs/e2e-lifecycle.md`: the rule the team should follow for how a spec
   starts. It needs to be specific enough that the next person does not
   rediscover Dana's afternoon.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `e2e/init.js` so the suite no longer reinstalls the app before every
   spec.
2. Edit any spec files that need to change as a consequence of that.
3. Write `docs/e2e-lifecycle.md`: the rule the team should follow for how a spec
   starts. It needs to be specific enough that the next person does not
   rediscover Dana's afternoon.
assertions: MUST NOT leave a per-spec uninstall-and-install in e2e/init.js; the reinstall is 1m52s of every spec's runtime and a JS reload of the running app buys the same isolation for 0.8s. Keeping the reinstall scores zero. A full cold relaunch in the shared hook rather than a reload scores at most half — it is eight times the cost for the same result, by the report's own instrumentation.

e2e/onboarding.test.js must end up starting from a genuinely fresh install of its own, not from the shared reload rule. Its 'seen' flag lives in device storage, so it outlives a JS reload and only a reinstall clears it: the first spec expects to find a tour that will not be there. Leaving that file to run under the shared reload rule with no fresh-install launch of its own scores zero. Giving it a launch without saying why — that persisted storage survives a reload and the tour is a once-per-install behaviour — scores at most half. Deleting, skipping or rewriting the file to dodge the problem scores zero.

The two deep-link specs must keep starting the app from the URL themselves; being started by the link is the behaviour under test, and Dana's log shows both specs landing on home when the app is already running. Removing or replacing their own launches in pursuit of a single uniform rule scores zero. Keeping them but not explaining in docs/e2e-lifecycle.md why this file is different scores at most half.

Both permissions specs must keep launching with their own permission state. Full marks additionally require noticing that Dana's run is not evidence of safety for the second spec: only the first is listed as failing, but the grant never took effect in her run, the banner was visible in both cases, and 'shows the banner when denied' passed without testing anything. Restoring the launches without that observation scores at most half. Letting either spec run under the shared rule scores zero.

MUST NOT introduce fixed-duration sleeps between actions or in the shared hooks as a way of steadying the suite after the reinstall comes out, and MUST NOT keep a reinstall in any file that does not need one. Either scores zero. Adding retries to paper over the order-dependence scores at most half.
docs/e2e-lifecycle.md exists and states the default rule for how a spec starts plus every file that departs from it and why. A document that states only the default rule scores at most half.
MUST NOT modify e2e/browse.test.js or e2e/cart.test.js; both are correct under the new shared rule and neither was part of the failure. Any edit to either scores zero here.

# The reorder spec cannot reach the row it needs, and the fix on the table slows the app down

## Problem Description

We shipped "reorder" last sprint — open an old order from the history list, tap
Reorder, the basket refills. QA wrote one end-to-end spec for it against our
React Native app and it has never passed. Two different errors, one after the
other, and both are in the attached log.

Vik's PR #901 makes both go away. It sets the history list to render a hundred
rows up front and turns off clipping of off-screen children, and it adds a
helper to the spec that scrolls eight times with a pause after each scroll. The
spec is green in six minutes.

Nadia, our performance lead, has measured the branch. Time-to-interactive on the
history screen goes from 240ms to 1.9s on the Pixel 6a, against a 400ms budget,
on the second most visited screen in the app. She has put a hold on production
changes to that screen for the rest of the sprint and she is not going to lift
it for a test.

Vik says that leaves him nowhere: the row the spec needs does not exist until
the list renders it, and the list will not render it. He has been at this for
four days and the spec has to land this week.

Work out what actually has to change, and give me something I can send to both
of them. The spec, the two components, both failure runs, the performance
numbers and Vik's patch are attached, along with the sorting module the screen
uses and its unit tests.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `e2e/reorder.test.js` so both errors are gone.
2. Change `app/OrderHistoryScreen.jsx` or `app/OrderRow.jsx` if your fix needs
   it.
3. Write `docs/pr-901-review.md`: the review Vik and Nadia both get. Cover each
   of the two errors separately, say what is landing and what is not, and say
   what Vik should do instead of what he has done.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `e2e/reorder.test.js` so both errors are gone.
2. Change `app/OrderHistoryScreen.jsx` or `app/OrderRow.jsx` if your fix needs
   it.
3. Write `docs/pr-901-review.md`: the review Vik and Nadia both get. Cover each
   of the two errors separately, say what is landing and what is not, and say
   what Vik should do instead of what he has done.
assertions: e2e/reorder.test.js is rewritten and docs/pr-901-review.md exists. A review that does not separate the two errors scores at most half.

Reaching order 1042 must use the runner's wait construct with the scroll supplied as the action it performs while the condition is unmet, scoped to the history list and bounded by a timeout. A hand-rolled loop over a fixed number of scrolls scores zero even if it would pass today; so does a fixed sequence of scroll calls, any sleep between scrolls, and scrolling to the end of the list and hoping the row is on screen. Using the construct but with no timeout on it, or aimed at the screen rather than the scrollable list, scores at most half.

MUST NOT put `initialNumToRender`, `windowSize` or `removeClippedSubviews` into app/OrderHistoryScreen.jsx, or otherwise make the list render rows it would not otherwise render. Any of them appearing scores zero regardless of the rest. Full marks require the review to say why in Nadia's terms — 240ms to 1.9s against a 400ms budget on 18.4% of sessions — rather than 'because it was blocked'.

app/OrderRow.jsx must end up giving each row an identifier derived from the order id, so a single row can be named without counting. Leaving the component untouched — treating the hold as covering every change to the screen — scores zero, because the spec then still has nothing to match on. Making the change without telling Nadia what it is and why it is not the thing she measured (no change to what renders, or when) scores at most half. Achieving uniqueness by combining the existing matcher with something else about the row, rather than an id, scores at most half.

MUST NOT leave `atIndex(30)`, or any other positional index, as the way the second and third specs select order 1042 — the QA notes say that row becomes the 44th next quarter. Any positional selection of 1042 surviving scores zero. Using an index for `the most recent order`, which is defined by its position, is acceptable and does not score zero here.

docs/pr-901-review.md must give Vik a concrete replacement for each of the two errors, not only a verdict on his patch. A review that rejects PR #901 without stating what he does instead scores zero. Stating the replacement without connecting it to the growing account, so the reader can see why it does not expire, scores at most half.
MUST NOT modify src/order-history.js or test/order-history.test.js; the ordering is correct and is not implicated in either failure. Any edit to either scores zero here.

evals.prompt:
# The whole mobile suite froze the day pull-to-refresh landed

## Problem Description

Larder (React Native, iOS + Android) had a fourteen-spec end-to-end suite that
ran in about four minutes and had been boring for a year. Sprint 44 merged two
things on the same afternoon:

- a pull-to-refresh spinner on the orders list, and
- a telemetry stream that keeps a long-poll open to
  `https://telemetry.larder.internal/v1/telemetry/stream` for session analytics.

Since that merge **every one of the fourteen specs fails**, and they all fail the
same way: the first `tap()` in the spec never completes, and two minutes later
the runner kills it. Not a single spec gets to its assertions. Nobody touched
the specs — `git log e2e/` has no commits in six weeks. It reproduces on every
developer's machine and on both CI runners, iOS and Android alike, first try,
every time.

Aleks has PR #812 open and it works: the suite is green in three minutes and
eight seconds, three people have approved it, and code freeze is Friday. He is
not being lazy, he is being pragmatic — a red suite blocks the release train and
nobody else has produced anything at all. I am the one who has to press the
button and I would rather press it than explain to the release manager why we
slipped. Talk me out of it, or tell me to merge it.

Separately: Ines has had a branch open since June with one spec for the live
tracking map. It has never passed. It fails the same way the fourteen do now,
except it was doing it three months before sprint 44, and it is the only spec
that ever did. We left it on the branch and forgot about it. Her spec, the
screen it drives and the vendor notes for the map package are attached with
everything else, and I would like an answer on that too while we are here.

The timeout logs, the new app code, the current global setup, one representative
spec and Aleks's patch are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/rca-suite-freeze.md` — what is blocking the taps, what introduced
   it, and your verdict on PR #812 with the reasoning behind it.
2. Make the edits you are recommending: to `e2e/init.js`, to the app source, or
   to both. Leave `e2e/orders.test.js` alone unless your fix genuinely requires a
   change inside it.
3. Say what should happen to Ines's branch.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/rca-suite-freeze.md` — what is blocking the taps, what introduced
   it, and your verdict on PR #812 with the reasoning behind it.
2. Make the edits you are recommending: to `e2e/init.js`, to the app source, or
   to both. Leave `e2e/orders.test.js` alone unless your fix genuinely requires a
   change inside it.
3. Say what should happen to Ines's branch.
assertions: docs/rca-suite-freeze.md exists, and the recommended edits are actually made rather than only described. A document with no corresponding edits scores at most half.

Full marks require identifying that app/RefreshSpinner.jsx starts a looping animation in an effect that does not depend on `refreshing`, that OrdersScreen mounts it unconditionally and only hides it with opacity, and fixing it so the loop runs only while a refresh is actually in progress — stopping it, or not mounting the component, when it is not. Naming the animation but only working around it from the test layer scores zero. Hiding the spinner differently, or setting `useNativeDriver: false`, without stopping the loop scores zero, because the animation is still running. Stopping the loop without saying why a permanently-animating view stalls every action scores at most half.

Full marks require recognising that the telemetry stream is re-opened the moment it closes, so there is always a request in flight, and taking that traffic out of what the suite waits on — excluding that host or URL from the tracked set for the run, or not starting the stream in the end-to-end build. Removing the feature, shortening the server's hold, or otherwise changing what real users get in order to make the suite pass scores zero. Leaving the long-poll unaddressed because the animation was fixed scores zero — the log lists both, and the suite still stalls on the request alone.

MUST NOT turn the runner's idle waiting off for the whole run, and MUST NOT put fixed pauses into the shared hooks or the specs. Endorsing #812, or endorsing it as a temporary measure to be revisited after the freeze, scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require saying what the suite loses: with the wait suspended globally every action fires blind and every spec now depends on a hardcoded pause being longer than whatever the app happens to be doing on that runner.

Her spec is the case where suspending the idle wait IS the right answer: the animation belongs to a third-party native module, the vendor notes say it runs for as long as the view is mounted with no way to stop it, and it predates sprint 44. Full marks require suspending the wait only around the map interaction and restoring it immediately afterwards, with explicit waits used inside that window, plus the reason it is allowed here and not in #812. Refusing the escape hatch everywhere and leaving her spec broken scores zero. Suspending it for the whole file, or for the whole run, scores at most half. Recommending the same treatment for the fourteen specs scores zero.

MUST NOT modify app/CartBadge.jsx, whose animation is a bounded sequence that finishes, and MUST NOT modify src/backoff.js or test/backoff.test.js, which are correct and are not implicated. Editing e2e/orders.test.js at all, when no fix requires it, scores zero here.
